items.title: WWI was triggered by a wrong turn
items.claim: On 28 June 1914, Archduke Franz Ferdinand survived the first assassination attempt that morning. What caused the second, successful attempt hours later?

options.text: A coordinated second wave of assassins ambushed his motorcade on the way to the hospital
His driver took a wrong turn into a side street, stalled the car, and stopped directly in front of Gavrilo Princip
Princip followed the motorcade by tram and intercepted it at the town hall
A Serbian double agent inside the security detail signalled his location

items.reveal_title: A wrong turn into world war
items.reveal:
After a bomb attack that morning failed, the Archduke insisted on visiting the wounded at the hospital. His driver, Leopold Lojka, had not been told the route had been changed. He turned right onto Franz Joseph Street, was told he was going the wrong way, and stalled while reversing.

Gavrilo Princip, who had given up and was eating a sandwich (the sandwich story is disputed but he was at Schiller's delicatessen), happened to be standing there. He stepped forward and fired twice from five feet away.
items.why: The 'causes of WWI' essay tends to load every variable onto structural forces (alliances, militarism, imperialism). Those forces created the powder keg, but a stalled car lit the fuse. Contingency matters.

items.title: Tutankhamun was minor — fame comes from an intact tomb
items.claim: Why is Tutankhamun (r. c. 1332-1323 BCE) so famous?

options.text: He was the greatest of all New Kingdom pharaohs
He was a young, minor pharaoh whose tomb (KV62) was found nearly intact by Howard Carter on 4 November 1922 — almost the only royal tomb to escape ancient looting
He led the Egyptians to defeat the Hittites
He was the first pharaoh to build a pyramid

items.reveal:
Tutankhamun died around age 19 after a reign of about 9 years. He partially reversed his father Akhenaten's religious reforms but his reign was historically minor.

Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found a single step on 4 November 1922 after years of fruitless digging. On 26 November he made a small hole, held up a candle, and when asked if he could see anything famously replied 'Yes, wonderful things'. The tomb contained over 5,000 artefacts. Carnarvon died of an infected mosquito bite in April 1923, fuelling 'curse' stories.
items.why: Fame is not the same as historical importance. Tutankhamun's celebrity is an artefact of preservation and 20th-century media, not of what he actually did.

items.title: The US Vietnam draft was decided by a televised lottery
items.claim: How was the Vietnam draft (Selective Service) administered after 1969?

options.text: Strict order by date of birth, alphabetical
On 1 December 1969, blue capsules with birthdates were drawn from a glass jar on national TV — men born on dates drawn first were called up first
By state quota with each state choosing its own method

items.reveal:
The 1 December 1969 lottery selected 19-26 year olds. 366 capsules (one per birthday including 29 February) were drawn live. Men with low numbers (1-195) were called; high numbers (typically 196+) were spared.

The statistical method was later shown to have biased the draw — capsules added in order from January were less thoroughly mixed, so December birthdays were over-represented at low numbers.

Deferments before 1969 — for university students, for medical reasons — disproportionately spared the wealthy. Around 2.7 million Americans served in Vietnam; 58,220 died. The draft ended in 1973.
items.why: Even apparently neutral mechanisms encode injustice. The Vietnam draft's class bias before 1969, and the statistical bias of the 1969 lottery itself, are case studies in how 'fairness' breaks down in practice.
